title: Project folder structure
plain: A project is one folder that holds everything a program needs: its code (often in a src folder), a README, config files and tests. The top folder is the project root.
check: You ask Codex to add a new page and it proposes a new file in the project root. What do you look at in the existing folders before you accept, and why?
rubric: Names the project root and shows where it is (the path printed by pwd, or the top of the editor's explorer)
Says what the code folder, the README and one config file are for
Points to one folder that is generated or managed by tools and should not be edited by hand (for example node_modules or .git)
try: Open your project folder in your code editor and look at the file list on the left. Pick four top-level items (for example README.md, a code folder, a config file and a folder you do not know) and write one sentence for each saying what it is for. Open README.md first: it usually says what the project is and how to run it.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any file can go anywhere, because the computer does not care about the layout. Correct idea: tools expect certain names and places (README.md, .gitignore and package files at the root, code in a code folder), and a steady layout helps people and AI find things, so follow the layout that is already there.

title: File extensions and types
plain: A file extension is the ending of a file name, such as .py or .png, that labels the kind of content. Text files hold readable characters; binary files, such as images and programs, do not.
check: You rename `photo.png` to `photo.txt` and open it in a text editor. What do you expect to see, and why did the rename not turn the picture into text?
rubric: Sorts .py, .js, .md, .json and .txt as text, and .png, .jpg, .zip, .pdf and .exe as binary
Predicts that renaming changes only the label, not the content
Explains that a binary file opened in a text editor shows unreadable symbols
try: In a project folder that has an image, run `python -c "print(open('logo.png','rb').read(4))"` (python3 on macOS and Linux), with your own image file name instead of logo.png. A PNG file prints b'\x89PNG', which is unreadable. Run the same line with README.md: the output is readable letters. Use `ls` first to see the real file names and their extensions.
pitfall: Wrong belief: renaming a file to .txt or .pdf converts it. Correct idea: the extension is only a label; the content stays the same, so a renamed picture is still a picture and may not open, and to convert a file you re-save it in the new format with a program.

title: Code editor
plain: A code editor (such as VS Code) is a program for reading and changing text files, with colors for code. Edits reach the file on disk when you save; the terminal is for running commands.
check: You added a line to `app.py` in the editor and ran `python app.py` in the terminal, but the output did not change. What are two possible reasons?
rubric: Edits and saves with the keyboard shortcut (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on macOS)
Spots the sign of unsaved changes in the editor (many editors show a dot on the tab)
Confirms what is on disk from the terminal with cat file-name
try: In your editor create `notes.txt` in a scratch folder with the line `first` and save it. Add a second line `second` but do not save. In the terminal, in the same folder, run `cat notes.txt`: it shows only first. Save with Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) and run it again: both lines appear.
pitfall: Wrong belief: what I see in the editor is what the program will run. Correct idea: programs read the saved file on disk; unsaved text exists only in the editor window.

title: Config files
plain: A config file stores settings for a tool or project as plain text. Common formats are JSON (braces and quotes), YAML (indented lines), TOML (key = value lines) and .env (NAME=value lines).
check: A tool refuses to start and prints an error about your package.json that names line 12, column 3. What do you check first, and what are two common mistakes that cause JSON errors?
rubric: Uses the line and column in the error message to find the exact place
States the JSON rules that were broken (double quotes, commas between items, none after the last item, no comments)
Checks the file again with python -m json.tool or the editor's problem list after the fix
try: In your editor create `bad.json` in a scratch folder with this content: { "name": "demo", "count": 3, } and save it. Run `python -m json.tool bad.json` (python3 on macOS and Linux). It prints an error that names line 1 and a column; newer Python versions say Illegal trailing comma before end of object, older ones say Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes. Delete the comma after 3, save, and run it again: the formatted JSON is printed.
pitfall: Wrong belief: config formats are interchangeable and forgiving. Correct idea: each has strict rules: strict JSON allows no comments and no comma after the last item, YAML shows structure with spaces (never tabs), and .env files are read by tools with slightly different rules; one wrong character can stop the tool.

title: Markdown
plain: Markdown is a way to format plain text with simple symbols: # for headings, - for bullet lists, ** for bold, and backticks for code. Files ending in .md use it, such as README.md.
check: Your README shows `**install**` with the stars visible instead of bold text. What are two possible reasons?
rubric: Gives two causes: the text is shown where no Markdown viewer runs, or a space or a missing closing ** just inside the stars stops the bold
Uses # for a heading, - for list items, and a fenced code block that starts and ends with three backticks
Opens a preview and fixes one thing that does not look as intended
try: In a scratch folder create `notes.md` with a first line `# My notes`, an empty line, then two lines `- first item` and `- second item`. Open the editor's Markdown preview (in VS Code: Ctrl+Shift+V, or Cmd+Shift+V on macOS). You see a large heading and a bullet list instead of the symbols.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Markdown is a program or a Word-like file format. Correct idea: it is plain text with symbols; the formatted look comes from a viewer, such as an editor preview or GitHub, and without a viewer you see the symbols.

title: Hidden files (dotfiles)
plain: Hidden files are not shown in file lists by default. On macOS and Linux this means names that start with a dot (.env, .gitignore). Show them with `ls -a`, or in PowerShell with `ls -Force`.
check: Your project folder looks empty in the file explorer, yet Codex says it edited `.env`. How can you see that file, and why is it worth knowing that it exists?
rubric: Uses the right option for their shell (ls -a, or ls -Force in PowerShell)
Names .git and one other dotfile such as .gitignore or .env, and says what each does
Says why such files exist (settings and history that tools use, not content to edit casually)
try: In your project folder run `ls -a` (PowerShell: `ls -Force`) and compare it with `ls`: the extra names start with a dot, for example .git or .gitignore. If .gitignore exists, read it with `cat .gitignore`. Both commands only read and change nothing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if I cannot see a file, it is not there or does not matter. Correct idea: hidden files hold settings, secrets (.env) and the whole Git history (.git), so never delete or share them without knowing what they are; on Windows a leading dot alone does not hide a file, and Git for Windows marks only the .git folder as hidden by default.

title: Line endings and UTF-8
plain: Text files store characters as bytes using an encoding; UTF-8 is the common standard. Each line ends with an invisible code: LF on macOS and Linux, often CRLF on Windows. Mismatches can break tools.
check: A file made with `echo hi > a.txt` in Windows PowerShell 5.1 fails when Python reads it as UTF-8, with `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0`. What does the byte 0xff tell you, and what are two ways to fix it?
rubric: Says the file's bytes are not UTF-8 text; 0xff 0xfe at the start marks UTF-16
Fixes it on the reading side (encoding='utf-16') or by saving the file again as UTF-8
Checks the encoding and line ending shown in the editor's status bar
try: Open a text file in your editor and read the status bar: many editors show the file's encoding (for example UTF-8) and its line ending (LF or CRLF). Then look at the raw bytes: `python -c "print(open('README.md','rb').read(60))"` (python3 on macOS and Linux). A \r\n in the output marks a CRLF line ending; a single \n marks LF.
pitfall: Wrong belief: text is only text, so a file is read the same way everywhere. Correct idea: the same characters can be stored with different encodings and line endings, so write UTF-8 and ask for it, as in open(path, encoding='utf-8') in Python (before Python 3.15 the default follows the computer's settings). In your own Windows PowerShell 5.1 window > saves UTF-16, while PowerShell 7 saves UTF-8. Check how a file was saved before a program or Git reads it.

title: Synced folders (OneDrive)
signals: where should i put my project
plain: A synced folder (OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive) is copied to the cloud automatically. This copy is not a Git history, and it can clash with the hidden .git folder inside a project.
check: A friend says: 'My project is inside OneDrive, so it is backed up and I do not need Git.' What is true in that sentence, and what is missing?
rubric: Reads the project path and names any synced folder in it (OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive, Google Drive)
Explains that sync mirrors files, including deletions and half-finished changes, while a Git commit records a named snapshot
Names a safer setup: the project in an unsynced folder, history in Git, and a remote copy on GitHub as the backup
try: Run `pwd` in your project folder and read the path. Does it contain OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud or Google Drive? On Windows, Desktop and Documents are often inside a OneDrive folder; on macOS, iCloud Drive can also store the Desktop and Documents folders, so check your iCloud Drive settings too. This step only reads; decide about moving the project together with your tutor.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a folder that syncs to the cloud is a backup of my project's history, so Git is optional. Correct idea: sync copies every change and every deletion, including a broken state, and users report corrupted Git repositories and conflict copies when a repository sits in a synced folder; keep projects in an unsynced folder and use Git commits plus a remote repository for history and backup.
